first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-mechanical (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and simplify_onboarding is the one lever whose inherited evidence (memory_31 signup-field reduction, memory_86 shortened onboarding) speaks directly to both, without the margin and selection risk that a discount response carries. I am spending both verification pulls on memory_31 and memory_86 precisely because they are the load-bearing basis for my intended action and because both are consolidated summaries whose phrasing ('activation', 'completion', 'early adoption') describes upstream funnel metrics only — the archived records need to show whether the original experiments ever measured downstream qualified revenue, retention, or lead quality, or whether friction removal simply admitted lower-intent accounts that never converted. That is the specific failure mode against the stated objective: a real activation lift that is value-neutral or value-negative further down the funnel. I did not verify memory_73 (promotional pricing) because even if it fully replicates, matching a competitor's entry pricing buys price-sensitive volume of exactly the kind least likely to become sustainable qualified revenue, so verification would not change my choice; memory_91 (activation messaging) is my fallback if the archive undercuts the onboarding records, and memory_44/memory_57 address segments that are not the source of the current decline. Running as a standard experiment with a holdout rather than a broad rollout, with downstream qualified-revenue and retention guardrails instrumented alongside completion rate, so that an upstream lift alone does not license a rollout. If the archive reveals the original studies stopped at activation, I will treat these memories as unproven on the metric that matters and size down to a guarded test.

final.rationale: The archive largely answers the question I was worried about. exp_31 did not stop at the upstream metric: it carried through to qualified revenue (+4%) with only a -1% 30-day retention move, so the activation lift there was not purely the admission of low-intent signups. exp_86 confirms completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days with retention actually positive (+3%), though it never measured qualified revenue at all — so the revenue case rests on exp_31 alone, and I am treating exp_86 as evidence that the mechanism does not damage retention rather than as independent evidence of value. Committing the slot to simplify_onboarding: it is the only lever with verified downstream-revenue evidence, and it addresses both declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) at their mechanical source rather than buying volume. Two limits I am carrying forward rather than papering over. First, exp_31 explicitly did not replicate outside SMB, so I scope this to SMB self-serve and make no claim about enterprise, where memory_44's sales-assisted path remains the better-supported route. Second, both records are stale relative to the current situation (day 12 and day 52, versus a day-76 environment with an aggressive competitor now taking price-sensitive SMB accounts); the population entering the funnel this week may be more price-shopping and less intent-qualified than the population those experiments measured, which is exactly the condition under which a friction-removal lift could show up in completion and evaporate in revenue. So: standard experiment with a holdout, not a broad rollout, powered on completion and activation but with qualified revenue and 30-day retention instrumented as gating guardrails, and the small negative retention signal from exp_31 watched specifically for amplification under the new mix. An upstream lift alone does not license a rollout. I declined to spend the slot on promotional_pricing despite memory_73 because matching entry pricing recruits precisely the accounts least likely to become sustainable qualified revenue, and I never verified that record; activation_messaging (memory_91) remains the unverified fallback if this reads out flat.
